instruction: What is the recommended planting spacing for maize in a rain-fed smallholder farm?
output: For rain-fed smallholder maize, plant in rows 75 cm apart with plants 25 cm apart within the row, sowing one seed per station. This gives roughly 53,000 plants per hectare, a good target for rain-fed conditions. If moisture is very limited, widen the in-row spacing to 30 cm to reduce competition for water. Plant 2-5 cm deep into moist soil and thin to one healthy plant per station if you sow more than one seed.

instruction: How do I identify and manage fall armyworm in maize?
output: Identify it by ragged, elongated holes in young leaves and moist, sawdust-like frass packed in the whorl. The caterpillar has a pale inverted 'Y' on its head and four dark spots forming a square on the second-to-last body segment. Manage it with an integrated approach: (1) scout fields at least twice a week from emergence, especially the whorl; (2) plant early and uniformly with your neighbours so the crop passes the vulnerable stage together; (3) crush egg masses and young larvae by hand or apply a pinch of dry sand or ash into infested whorls; (4) use biopesticides such as Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or neem, applied into the whorl in the cool of early morning or evening; (5) conserve natural enemies (ants, earwigs, parasitic wasps) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; (6) use a push-pull system with a legume intercrop and a Napier grass border where possible. Reserve synthetic insecticides for when damage is severe, rotate the active ingredients, and always follow label safety.

instruction: When and how should I top-dress maize with nitrogen fertilizer?
output: Top-dress nitrogen when maize is about knee-high, roughly 4-6 weeks after emergence, when the plant's demand rises fast. Use urea or CAN, placing it in a band about 5-10 cm to the side of the row and covering it with soil so it is not lost to the air. Apply to moist soil, ideally just before expected rain. If your rate is high, split it into two doses (knee-high and just before tasseling) to reduce loss and match crop uptake.

instruction: My cassava leaves show yellow-and-green mosaic patterns and are distorted. What is wrong and what should I do?
output: That pattern is classic cassava mosaic disease, a virus spread by whitefly and, most importantly, through infected planting cuttings. It cannot be cured once a plant is infected. To manage it: uproot and destroy severely affected plants, take cuttings only from healthy, vigorous plants (or use certified clean material), and plant tolerant or resistant varieties suited to your area. Keep fields weeded and well nourished so plants can tolerate mild infection, and avoid moving cuttings from clearly diseased fields to new ones.

instruction: Purple-flowered witchweed (Striga) is choking my sorghum. How do I control it?
output: Striga is a parasitic weed that attaches to cereal roots and drains the crop, and it thrives on poor, low-nitrogen soils. Control it over several seasons: (1) improve soil fertility with manure, compost, or nitrogen fertilizer, which suppresses Striga; (2) rotate or intercrop with legumes such as cowpea, groundnut, or soybean, whose root chemicals trigger Striga to germinate without a host so it dies; (3) hand-pull and burn Striga before it flowers and sets seed to run down the huge seed bank; (4) use Striga-tolerant or resistant cereal varieties where available. Consistency across seasons matters more than any single treatment because the seeds survive many years in the soil.

instruction: How can I store my maize harvest to avoid weevil damage without chemicals?
output: First dry the grain well, to about 13% moisture or lower, so it is hard and cracks rather than dents when bitten. Then use hermetic (airtight) storage such as PICS triple-layer bags or a sealed metal silo: sealed insects use up the oxygen and die, and no insecticide is needed. Fill and seal the bags fully, keep them off the floor and away from walls, and open them as little as possible. Clean the store and remove old infested grain before adding the new harvest. Good drying plus airtight storage also lowers the risk of aflatoxin-producing molds.

instruction: Many of my village chickens die suddenly, especially in the dry season. What could it be and what should I do?
output: Sudden mass deaths in village poultry are most often Newcastle disease, a highly contagious virus that spikes seasonally. There is no treatment once birds are sick, so prevention is key: vaccinate your flock routinely with a thermotolerant Newcastle vaccine (such as I-2), which many extension services distribute for local conditions. During an outbreak, separate sick birds, do not sell or move birds to other homes, and safely bury or burn dead birds instead of eating or discarding them in the open. Provide clean water, shelter, and secure night housing to reduce stress and other losses.

instruction: Why should I rotate my maize with beans or cowpea?
output: Legumes such as beans and cowpea host Rhizobium bacteria on their roots that fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, leaving residual nitrogen for the following maize crop and cutting your fertilizer need. Rotation also breaks the cycles of maize pests and diseases (like stemborers and some soil diseases) that build up under continuous maize, and the legume residues add organic matter that improves soil structure and water holding. For best effect, inoculate the legume seed with the right Rhizobium, and return the legume residues to the soil rather than removing or burning them.

instruction: How do I know when to plant maize for the rains?
output: Plant once the rainy season is reliably established, not at the very first shower, which can be followed by a dry spell that kills seedlings. A practical rule is to wait until the soil is moist to about 15-20 cm depth after two or three good rains, then plant into that moisture. Use a variety whose maturity length fits your season: short-duration varieties for shorter or less reliable rains, longer-duration ones only where rains are dependable. Planting early but on established rains, together with your neighbours, also helps the whole area escape the worst fall armyworm and reduces bird damage.

instruction: My area is getting hotter and drier. What crops should I consider instead of relying only on maize?
output: In hotter, drier conditions, spread your risk by including drought-tolerant cereals and legumes alongside maize. Sorghum and pearl millet handle heat and dry spells far better than maize and still provide staple grain. Cowpea, groundnut, and pigeon pea are drought-hardy legumes that also improve the soil. Cassava and sweet potato give a reliable fallback harvest when rains fail. Choose short-duration, improved varieties, practise conservation agriculture (minimum tillage with soil cover) to hold moisture, and intercrop cereals with legumes so a single poor rain does not wipe out your whole harvest.

instruction: What is aflatoxin and how do I keep it out of my maize and groundnuts?
output: Aflatoxin is a poison produced by Aspergillus molds that grow on maize and groundnuts when they are damaged, harvested late, or dried and stored while damp. It is harmful to people and animals and often cannot be seen or tasted. To keep it low: harvest on time, avoid leaving mature crop in the field or in contact with wet soil, dry the crop quickly on a raised rack or tarpaulin (not bare ground) to about 13% moisture, sort out moldy or damaged grain, and store in clean, dry, airtight containers off the ground. Where available, biocontrol products (such as Aflasafe) applied in the field also reduce contamination.

instruction: What is the difference between DAP and urea, and when do I use each on maize?
output: DAP (di-ammonium phosphate) supplies phosphorus plus some starter nitrogen and is applied at planting, placed in the planting hole or furrow and lightly separated from the seed, to drive strong early root growth. Urea is almost pure nitrogen and is used later as a top-dressing when the crop is knee-high to power leaf and stem growth and grain filling. In short: DAP at planting for roots and phosphorus, urea a few weeks later for nitrogen. Always apply to moist soil and cover the fertilizer to reduce loss.
